exp.0:6:
They say that many deceivers have gone out into the world, people who teach false things. They do not acknowledge that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, that is, as a real human being, with a true body. John says that whoever teaches this is a deceiver and an antichrist, a word that means someone who opposes Christ or teaches the opposite of what He is.

The one speaking is John, who presents himself as the elder (as verse 1 says; tradition identifies him with the apostle, though some dispute this). He writes to the lady, who may be a woman or a local church. Earlier he spoke of love and obedience; now he warns that true love cannot be separated from the truth about Jesus.

Today we can love everyone, but we should also examine what is taught, comparing it with what Jesus said and is according to the Bible.
exp.0:8:
Whoever goes beyond the teaching and does not remain in the teaching about Christ does not have God. But whoever remains in that teaching has both the Father and the Son. To remain firm means to hold on to it and not let it go.

The writer presents himself as the elder, traditionally identified with the apostle John, though some scholars debate this. He writes to a church, addressing it as the chosen lady and her children, and warns them about teachers who denied that Jesus came in the flesh. John wants to protect believers from deception.

For today: before following a teaching or a teacher, compare it with what Jesus and the apostles taught in the Bible. Stand firm in Christ, even when something new sounds attractive, and treat with love those who think differently.
exp.0:11:
He says he has many more things to tell them, but he would rather not write them down with paper and ink. Instead, he hopes to visit them and speak face to face, so that their joy may be complete.

The one speaking is the elder, as he identifies himself at the start of the letter, traditionally understood to be the apostle John, though some scholars debate this. He writes to a church, or to a Christian lady and her children, warning them about false teachers. He closes the letter with a wish to see them in person.

For today: some conversations cannot be replaced by a message or an email. Make time to visit, call, or share a coffee with someone from your church or family. Being present strengthens friendship and faith, and brings a joy that screens rarely give.
exp.0:10:
It says that whoever welcomes a false teacher, one who does not bring the teaching of Christ, joins him in his evil works. Greeting him in this verse is a way of welcoming him. Here, to "share in" means to take part, to be a partner, or to contribute to something. In other words, giving support to that person means taking part in what he does.

The writer is John, the apostle, already elderly, writing to a church (addressed as the chosen lady or chosen sister). Many traveling teachers moved from place to place and received lodging from believers. John warns that support should not be given to those who deny the truth about Christ, because that helps spread the error.

For today: be kind to everyone, but do not help or promote someone who teaches something contrary to Christ. Before supporting a ministry or a preacher, it is good to examine his teaching in the light of the Bible, with humility and love.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that true love shows itself in obedience: to love God is to live according to his commandments. "Walk" means to conduct one's life, and the instruction that you must walk in love means that you should live within that love. What is commanded is not new, for you had already heard it from the beginning, that is, from the time you received the message of Christ.

The writer presents himself as "the elder," traditionally identified with the apostle John, though the text does not give his name. He writes to "the elect lady" and her children, which may be a church or a believing woman; it is read in both ways. He reminds them of love and truth because deceivers were appearing who denied that Jesus came in the flesh.

For today: do not separate love from obedience. This week, choose a teaching of Jesus you already know, such as forgiving or serving, and put it into practice with a specific person.
exp.0:3:
John says he was overjoyed to find some of the children of the chosen lady walking in the truth. Walking in the truth means living according to what God teaches, not merely believing it. The word "found" means he came across them, and the commandment from the Father refers to what God has asked of his people.

The writer presents himself as "the elder" in verse 1, and early Christian tradition identifies him with the apostle John, though some scholars debate this. He writes to "the chosen lady and her children," which may be a woman with her family or a local church; it is not known for certain. John encourages them to remain in the truth and in love, and soon he will warn them against false teachers.

Today we can rejoice and encourage others when we see them live out their faith consistently. Take a moment this week to tell someone that the way they live inspires you to follow God.
exp.0:4:
The author asks the "dear lady" that we love one another. He is careful to say this is not a new command but one they have had from the beginning, that is, from the time they first came to know Christ. He urges her with warmth and affection.

The one writing is "the elder," as he introduces himself in verse 1, traditionally identified with John. He writes to a "lady" and to her children. Some believe she is a real woman; others believe the words refer to a local church. This cannot be known for certain. He reminds them of the basics because later he warns about deceivers who denied that Jesus came in the flesh.

For today: before looking for new or complicated things, practice simple love. Today, do something concrete for a brother or sister: call, forgive, serve, or help someone.
exp.0:0:
This verse is a greeting. A man who calls himself "the elder" writes to "the chosen lady and her children." He says he loves them "in the truth," meaning with sincere love, and that he is not alone in this: all who know the truth of the gospel love them too.

Traditionally, the author is thought to be the apostle John, although the letter does not give his name. The "chosen lady" may be a Christian woman with her family, or a way of speaking about a local church with its members. Scholars have understood it in both ways, and there is no certainty.

Today we can show sincere love toward other believers. Just as the elder did not love alone, our love can join that of the whole Christian community. Today, seek out someone from your church and encourage them with a call or a message.
exp.0:2:
The writer says he wants grace, mercy, and peace to be with his readers. These blessings come from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, called the Son of the Father. Grace is God's favor, which we do not earn; mercy is his compassion; peace is his well-being and the restored relationship he brings. All of this is to be lived out in truth and love.

The one writing presents himself simply as the elder. Tradition holds that he is the apostle John, although the text does not give his name. He writes to the chosen lady and her children. Some believe this is a woman, and others believe it refers to a local church. His greeting joins truth and love, and it prepares his call to walk in the truth and to love one another.

For today: do not separate truth from love. When you speak about what you believe, do it with respect and kindness, and when you love, do it without setting aside what God teaches.
exp.0:7:
Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded. Be careful and stay alert. "Reward" means a prize or recompense. "Full" means complete, with nothing missing.

The author presents himself as "the elder" in this letter, and tradition attributes it to the apostle John, though some scholars dispute this. He writes to a local church, which he calls "the chosen lady." He warns them about deceivers who denied that Jesus came in the flesh. He asks them to remain firm in the truth they received at the beginning.

For today: we should not take our faith for granted. It is wise to examine humbly what we believe, compare it with the teachings of Jesus in the Bible, and stay close to God and to a healthy community so that we do not drift away.
exp.0:1:
The verse says that the love of the writer toward the chosen lady and her children comes because of the truth. That truth abides in believers and will be with them forever. The phrase "abides in us" means the truth is present within them and remains there, and "forever" means without end.

The writer calls himself "the elder," and it is traditionally thought to be the apostle John. He writes to a chosen lady and her children. Some believe she was a real woman; others think it refers to a local church. This cannot be known for certain. John reminds them that Christian love rests on the truth of God, not on feelings alone.

For today: build your friendships and your church life on the truth of God's Word. Love sincerely, but also stand firm in what God has taught, trusting that his truth does not change or come to an end.
exp.0:9:
If anyone comes to you but does not bring the true teaching about Christ, do not welcome them into your home or even greet them. That is the sense of the verse: you should not take such a person in or offer them a friendly greeting, since doing so would support a message that contradicts who Jesus is.

The writer calls himself "the elder." Tradition identifies him as the apostle John, though the text itself does not give his name. He writes to a church, addressed as "the elect lady," to protect it from traveling teachers who denied the truth about Jesus. In that time, Christians hosted travelers, so giving lodging to a false teacher meant backing his work.

For today: love everyone, but do not help spread teachings that contradict Christ. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and be firm and kind at the same time.
exp.0:12:
The verse tells us that the children of a sister of the "chosen lady" send you greetings. "Sister" here means sister in a family or spiritual sense. "Chosen" means chosen by God. The letter closes with a greeting from those who share this bond.

The author calls himself "the elder" (v. 1), and tradition identifies him with the apostle John, though some scholars debate this. He writes to "the chosen lady and her children." She may be a real woman or a way of speaking about a local church; it is understood in both ways. If it is a church, the "children of your sister" would be the members of another sister congregation. The letter warns against welcoming false teachers and ends with this affectionate greeting.

For today: never underestimate a sincere greeting. Writing, calling, or greeting fellow believers encourages them and reminds us that we form one family in the faith, beyond distance.

sum.0: The elder warmly greets the "elect lady" and her children, and he is glad to find them walking in the truth. He reminds them of the command to love one another and to live according to God's commandments. He warns them against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and asks them to remain firm in the teaching of Christ.
